title: Infra that fixes itself, thanks to coding agents — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on Railway Autofix, a system where a coding agent automatically monitors infrastructure and opens PRs with fixes, making coding agents the primary subject. The system uses Open Code as a coding assistant for automated software engineering and Railway as a developer platform for deployment and monitoring. The system operates on deployed services in production and performs operational monitoring and automated remediation. Requires familiarity with workflows, durable execution, coding agents, and infrastructure monitoring concepts. The talk is a live demonstration walking through dashboards, workflows, and a real pull request. Claims are supported by transcript excerpts with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: The talk introduces Railway Autofix, a system where coding agents monitor infrastructure and automatically open pull requests with fixes when issues are detected. Abdelwahab begins by showing Railway dashboards with multiple buggy services: one with a memory leak showing continuously growing memory, another with 94% request error rate and multi-second response times, and a third with deceptively normal metrics but extremely slow database queries causing 30-second page loads. He contrasts traditional alert-based workflows—where engineers get paged and manually investigate—with his proposed approach where a coding agent handles investigation and fix generation automatically. The system architecture involves scheduled workflows that fetch application architecture, resource metrics, and HTTP metrics, then identify services exceeding thresholds. He prefers scheduled analysis of time slices over alert-based triggers to avoid noise from spiky workloads. Once affected services are identified, the system pulls additional context including HTTP logs, build logs, and deployment logs, compiling everything into a formatted architecture summary passed to the coding agent as markdown. The generate fix workflow uses AI analysis to produce a plan with debugging steps and recommendations, then creates a session on the coding agent—each session acting as its own chat per repository. The implementation uses Inngest for durable execution, providing automatic retries, step-level result caching, and resume-from-failure capabilities. For the coding agent, he uses Open Code, an open-source terminal-based AI agent with a server-client architecture enabling headless deployment. The demo walks through the monitor project health workflow showing parallel steps fetching database resources, CPU and memory metrics, and HTTP metrics for each service, then transitions to pull service context which gathers logs, and finally generate fix which analyzes data with AI, creates a plan, and opens a PR. The demo concludes with an actual pull request opened on GitHub containing a summary of changes, analysis summary, root causes, and what was fixed. The Open Code server runs on Railway with a Dockerfile installing tools like git and GitHub CLI. The complete code is available on GitHub.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Infrastructure Problems Demo
sections.summary: Abdelwahab shows Railway dashboard with buggy services: one with a memory leak, another with 94% error rate and multi-second response times, and a third with normal-looking metrics but extremely slow database queries causing 30-second page loads.

sections.title: Proposed Solution: Agent-Based Monitoring
sections.summary: Proposes a coding agent that monitors infrastructure and ships fixes automatically. Instead of getting alerts and investigating manually, engineers review pull requests. Describes scheduled workflows to fetch architecture, resource metrics, and HTTP metrics, then identify affected services.

sections.title: Scheduled vs Alert-Based and Context Gathering
sections.summary: Argues scheduled analysis of time slices is better than alert-based triggers to avoid noise. Describes pulling additional context like logs, scanning code for upstream providers, checking status pages, and writing a detailed plan for the agent to implement fixes and open a PR.

sections.title: Durable Execution with Inngest
sections.summary: Explains durable execution using Inngest, showing a video processing workflow example. Highlights automatic retries, step-level result caching, and resume-from-failure capabilities that make API calls to Railway reliable and cost-effective.

sections.title: Open Code Agent Setup
sections.summary: Introduces Open Code as an open-source terminal AI agent with server-client architecture. Shows the Dockerfile installing tools, git, and GitHub CLI. Demonstrates the server running on port 49496, the API on localhost 3000 with Inngest UI, and kicks off the monitor project health workflow.

sections.title: Monitor Project Health Workflow Details
sections.summary: Walks through the monitor project health workflow steps. First step fetches project architecture showing databases, services with repo locations, and volumes. Parallel steps gather database resources with CPU and memory summaries formatted for the coding agent. Memory at 31.96 GB out of 32 GB max signals high usage. HTTP metrics for each service show error rates for 400s and 500s, latency, and status counts. All data is compiled into formatted summaries passed to the pull service context function.

sections.title: Generate Fix and Pull Request Creation
sections.summary: Shows the pull service context function fetching HTTP logs, build logs, and deployment logs for affected services, with an architecture summary formatted as markdown. The generate fix workflow analyzes all data with AI to produce a debugging plan with steps and recommendations. A coding agent session is created per repository. The demo concludes with an actual pull request opened on GitHub containing a summary of changes, analysis summary, root causes, and what was fixed. Abdelwahab closes by pointing viewers to the GitHub repo and his X/Twitter for questions.
